lesson.title: f Prime of g Times g Prime: The Chain Rule in Prime Notation
lesson.summary: Differentiating a composite function f(g(x)) means differentiating the outside function at the inside function's value, then multiplying by the derivative of the inside function.
lesson.body:
When one function is plugged into another, so h(x) = f(g(x)), the two pieces cannot simply be differentiated separately and added or multiplied the way sums and products work. Composition changes the input to f before f ever acts, so a change in x first gets reshaped by g and only then felt by f. The composition derivative rule captures this two stage effect precisely, and it is the prime notation counterpart to the Leibniz chain rule covered just before this topic; both describe the same underlying fact about how rates combine under composition.

The rule: if h(x) = f(g(x)), then h'(x) = f'(g(x)) times g'(x). Read f'(g(x)) as take the derivative function f', then evaluate it at g(x), not as differentiate g(x). That distinction trips up more students than any other part of the chain rule, so it is worth restating: f' is computed first as its own function, entirely independent of g, and only afterward is g(x) substituted in for its input. Skipping that order and instead differentiating g(x) itself as if it were the argument of f' produces a nonsensical expression that does not correspond to any valid derivative rule.

Let h(x) = sin(x^2). Here f(t) = sin(t) and g(x) = x^2. f'(t) = cos(t), so f'(g(x)) = cos(x^2). g'(x) = 2x. Therefore h'(x) = cos(x^2) times 2x = 2x cos(x^2). Verify with Leibniz notation as a second route: let u = x^2, y = sin(u). dy/du = cos(u) = cos(x^2), du/dx = 2x, so dy/dx = cos(x^2) times 2x, the same result reached a different way. A second worked example uses a different outside function: let h(x) = (2x+7)^4, so f(t) = t^4 and g(x) = 2x+7. f'(t) = 4t^3, so f'(g(x)) = 4(2x+7)^3, and g'(x) = 2, giving h'(x) = 8(2x+7)^3, a result that can be double checked by expanding (2x+7)^4 for small cases or by recognizing it as an instance of the power chain rule discussed next in this chapter.

A common error is to instead compute f(g'(x)), swapping the order of differentiate then substitute. For the sine example that mistake would give sin(2x) instead of 2x cos(x^2), a completely different function; checking at x = 1 shows the difference clearly, since the correct derivative is 2cos(1), approximately 1.0806, while the erroneous sin(2) is approximately 0.9093, so the two answers plainly disagree. This kind of numerical spot check, plugging a specific value into both the correct and the suspected wrong formula, is a fast way to catch an order-of-operations mistake before it propagates into a longer problem.

This rule is the engine behind every specialized chain rule that follows in this chapter: the power chain rule is just this formula with f(t) = t^n, the trig chain rule is this formula with f being sine, cosine, or another trig function, the exponential chain rule uses f(t) = e^t, and the log chain rule uses f(t) = ln(t). Mastering f'(g(x)) times g'(x) as one reusable pattern, rather than memorizing a separate rule per outside function, is what makes the rest of this chapter feel like variations on one theme instead of a dozen unrelated facts.
